title: Welcoming Shabbat
hookLine: six psalms for six weekdays, begun by the mystics of Safed who went out to greet the day

cards: Late Friday afternoon, in a hill town in the Galilee, in the 1500s. A group of scholars and mystics put on white clothes and walk out past the last houses, into the fields, as the sun drops toward the sea.
They aren't going anywhere. They're going out to meet someone. The town is Safed, home to a well-known circle of Jewish mystics, and the someone they're walking out to greet is the Sabbath itself.
Almost every synagogue's Friday night service still carries the shape of that walk.

teach.h: GO OUT TO GREET THE QUEEN.
teach.b: Kabbalat Shabbat means receiving, or welcoming, the Sabbath. The idea is old. The Talmud tells of a sage who wrapped himself in his cloak at sundown on Friday and said: come, let us go out to greet Shabbat the Queen.
But the service with that name took shape in Safed, in the sixteenth century, among the circle of kabbalists there, and from them it spread around the Jewish world.

Its backbone is six psalms, ninety-five through ninety-nine, and twenty-nine: one for each of the six weekdays that have just ended. You walk back through the week, psalm by psalm, before you step into the seventh day.
The first is a summons. In the old Jewish translation, Psalm 95 begins: "O come, let us sing unto the LORD; let us shout for joy to the Rock of our salvation."
The last, Psalm 29, is a thunderstorm: the voice of the LORD, seven times over, upon the waters, breaking the cedars, shaking the wilderness.
And then it ends with one word: peace. After the storm of the week, peace. Some say the seven voices match the seven blessings of the Friday night Amidah.
Then comes a song, which is tomorrow's lesson, and then the two psalms that belonged to Shabbat long before Safed.
Notice the posture. Shabbat isn't a day you fall into when you're tired. It's someone you go out to meet, dressed for it, on time.

how: Kabbalat Shabbat is the Friday evening service before Maariv in most communities: Psalms 95–99 and 29, the song Lecha Dodi, then Psalms 92 and 93. Many congregations sing it, and some still begin it outdoors.

games.q: you're a mystic in Safed. the sun is setting on Friday. where do you go?
o: out into the fields, dressed in white, to greet the Sabbath.
to the market for last-minute shopping.
games.why: the mystics went out past the town to meet Shabbat, and their walk became the welcoming service.

practice: Look back at your week one day at a time, the way the six psalms do, and take just one image from each day so far.
Then, if you'd like, read Psalm 95 or 29 slowly, or simply say its first line, O come, let us sing, and picture yourself walking out to meet the evening.
